title: What’s an SLO? How support teams can track service level objectives
summary: Learn what an SLO is, why B2B support teams use it, and how to set and track response time targets across channels like Slack and live chat.
body_markdown:
Support tickets constantly stream in through Slack, email, chat, and Microsoft Teams, and each one needs a timely response. While[multichannel support](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/multi-channel-b2b-support-software-vs-legacy-tools) gives B2B customers more ways to get help, it also makes it harder for your team to track all those requests.


Service level objectives (SLOs) can give your support team clear targets when responding to tickets. In this guide, you’ll learn what an SLO is, the benefits it offers, why manual workflows fall short, and how to[streamline tracking with Pylon](https://www.usepylon.com/analytics-reporting) .


## What’s an SLO?


Account customs fields in Pylon


An SLO (which means service level objective) is an internal performance goal that defines the level of service a support team aims to deliver. Every useful SLO has three components: a[support metric](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-track-support-metrics) , a target, and a time window. For example, your team might set an SLO to respond to 90% of customer tickets in an average of 45 minutes over the next month.


SLOs are part of a broader support framework that also includes:


- **Service level indicators (SLIs).** An SLI measures actual performance against a target. If 92% of tickets get a first response within 45 minutes, your team meets the 90% SLO it set.
- [Service level agreements](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/team-sla) **(SLAs).** An SLA defines the service commitment made to customers, like a guaranteed first response within 90 minutes. Unlike internal SLOs, SLAs are typically contractual, and they could include penalties or service credits when compliance isn’t met.


Together, these metrics show what the support team aims to achieve, how performance is measured, and what customers have been promised. For a more detailed comparison, check out our guide on SLOs versus SLAs and SLIs.


## How SLOs work in B2B customer support


Tracking business objectives through performance metrics shows your team what works and what needs to improve. This concept is common in site reliability engineering, where engineers use SLOs to track metrics like uptime and latency to keep systems running correctly.


The same concept applies to[B2B customer support](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/b2b-customer-service-best-practices-strategies) , but instead of tracking system performance, support teams set SLOs to spot delays and inefficiencies. Here are some common targets:


- **First response time:** How long a customer waits for the first reply from a support agent.
- **Next response time:** How long a customer waits after they reply to the first response.
- **Follow-up time:** How long it takes an agent to send an update before the customer reaches out again.
- **Resolution time:** How long it takes the support team to fully resolve an issue.


SLO targets should be shaped by factors like ticket priority and customer tier. An urgent issue, like a customer losing access to their account, could require a response within 15 minutes. On the other hand, a routine billing question may have a four-hour response target. And an enterprise-level customer on a premium support plan might need even stricter turnarounds.

You can[set different SLA targets](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/sla-best-practices) based on priority level, customize support hours, set up Slack alerts, and use reporting features to diagnose recurring issues.


## Why manual SLO tracking breaks down at scale


Triggers in Pylon


It’s easy to lose track of response time targets when your team[fields requests across Slack](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/slack-as-a-ticketing-system-2025) , Teams, email, and chat conversations. Without a shared view of incoming tickets, response deadlines can get overlooked, which makes it hard to consistently meet SLOs.


Disconnected channels also create confusion for complex B2B customer accounts. Without a shared record of earlier interactions, your team could waste time repeating work and hunting down context. And when data sits in separate systems, managers have to manually pull together response times and ticket counts.


Pylon brings conversations from all your support channels into one queue, which offers a more complete picture of SLO performance. With reliable reporting, you can identify repeat delays and see which types of requests consistently miss targets. Then, you can make informed decisions about staffing and ticket priorities to[improve the customer experience](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/effortless-customer-experience) .

## FAQ


### What happens if SLOs aren’t consistently met?


Missing an internal SLO doesn’t automatically breach an SLA, but repeated delays can put your compliance commitments at risk. Your team should review which targets they consistently miss, then use key metrics to find out if the problem involves staffing, ticket volume, data silos, or inefficient workflows.


### How do you choose appropriate SLIs?


Choose SLIs that reflect a fast, high-quality customer experience, and base them on the kinds of requests you get. For a support team handling urgent technical issues, resolution time may be more useful than first response time.


### What are service level objectives, and how do you measure them accurately?


SLOs are measurable targets you can use to track support performance. For instance, your team might aim to respond to 95% of urgent tickets within 10 minutes. To measure progress toward that goal, track when each ticket arrives and when the first customer-visible response is sent, then calculate the percentage of replies that meet the SLO.


### What happens if an SLA is breached?


An SLA breach happens when a provider fails to meet a customer commitment. Depending on the agreement terms, the consequences might include service credits or contractual penalties. Teams should diagnose the cause of each breach and address the issue across accounts to avoid repeats.
